analysis.one_liner: Gives the FDA authority to regulate cigarettes and other tobacco products.
analysis.headline: The bill became law: the House passed it 298-112, the Senate passed it 79-17, and the President signed it on June 22, 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: This law, for the first time, put cigarettes and other tobacco products under Food and Drug Administration oversight. The FDA can now inspect factories, review ingredients, ban candy-flavored cigarettes aimed at teens, require larger warning labels, and block misleading "light" or "less harmful" marketing. Companies pay user fees to cover the cost of regulation, and the law explicitly protects tobacco farms and growers from FDA authority and forbids banning cigarettes outright or setting the legal buying age above 18. A separate title adds automatic enrollment and a Roth option to federal employees' retirement savings plan.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and teenagers, who are targeted by candy-flavored products and youth-oriented advertising; current and future smokers, who get bigger warnings, honest labeling, and protection from false "reduced risk" claims; and the public generally, since the bill's findings note tobacco causes over 400,000 deaths a year. Federal employees also gain from automatic retirement-savings enrollment.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Teenagers, smokers, and the general public

how_it_helps.text: Puts tobacco under FDA regulation with annual factory registration, inspections every two years, ingredient disclosure, and recall authority [S3][S5].
Bans candy, fruit, and spice flavorings in cigarettes — strawberry, clove, grape, cinnamon and more — that are used to attract young smokers [S4].
Requires prominent new warning labels on packages and ads and lets the Secretary require color graphics depicting smoking's health consequences [S5][S6].
Prohibits "light," "mild," and "low tar" claims unless a product is scientifically proven to actually reduce harm, and bans advertising that implies FDA approval or safety [S3][S6].

Requires premarket approval of new tobacco products and lets the FDA restrict marketing and sales to protect public health, while funding enforcement through industry user fees rather than taxpayer dollars [S3][S6].
Automatically enrolls new federal employees in the Thrift Savings Plan at a 2-5% default contribution and adds a Roth option [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco manufacturers and importers, who bear compliance costs and pay quarterly user fees based on market share; retailers, who face advertising restrictions and possible no-tobacco-sale orders for repeat violations; and smokers, if industry compliance costs are passed on in prices.

drawbacks.text: Menthol is carved out of the flavor ban — the one flavor most used by African American smokers — and is only referred to a scientific advisory committee for study rather than restricted [S3][S5].

The law locks tobacco products in place: it forbids the FDA from banning cigarettes, smokeless tobacco, or cigars, from requiring nicotine to be reduced to zero, and from setting a purchase age above 18 [S3].

Critics warned that FDA regulation could imply tobacco products are federally vetted; the bill responds by banning claims that a product is approved, endorsed, or safer because it is FDA-regulated, but the risk of consumer confusion was a real concern [S6].
Compliance costs fall hardest on small manufacturers, whose testing and manufacturing-rule deadlines are delayed by years — a burden that tends to favor the largest firms [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health gain is large and direct: real authority over a product that kills hundreds of thousands of Americans a year, funded by industry fees. The costs are real but mostly private — compliance spending and fees that may raise cigarette prices, which most public health advocates would count as a benefit. The honest design flaws are the menthol exemption and the explicit prohibition on banning cigarettes or zeroing out nicotine, which means the industry's core products survive regulation intact.

outcome.mechanism: It passed both chambers with large bipartisan votes and the President signed it three weeks after the House agreed to the Senate's version.

narrative.text: Introduced March 3, 2009 by Rep. Henry Waxman, it was reported by two House committees within three weeks and passed the House 298-112 on April 2, 2009 [S10][S12].
The Senate needed a 60-vote procedural vote to start debating the bill; it cleared that easily, 84-11, on June 2, then passed an amended version 79-17 on June 11 [S10][S13][S15].
The House accepted the Senate amendment 307-97 on June 12, and the bill was signed into law as Public Law 111-31 on June 22, 2009 [S10][S16][S7].
Passage votes were lopsided but not unanimous: in the House, 228 of 253 Democrats and 70 of 178 Republicans voted yes; in the Senate, 23 of 40 Republicans voted yes on final passage [S12][S15].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary Americans gained the first federal regulatory authority over tobacco, and the largest cigarette manufacturers also came out ahead: the law entrenches the biggest firms' market position, exempts their tobacco suppliers, preserves menthol, and guarantees cigarettes cannot be banned. Smaller manufacturers faced the brunt of compliance costs.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Smokers and teens — and the biggest cigarette makers

sides.party_line_note: Democratic support was near-unanimous (228-8 in the House; 53-1 in the Senate on the first procedural vote), while Republicans split — 70 of 178 voted yes in the House and 23 of 40 on final Senate passage, but most Senate Republicans opposed even starting debate.

industries.note: The law regulates but also entrenches them: it bans candy flavors (not menthol), forbids the FDA from outlawing cigarettes or requiring zero nicotine, exempts tobacco growers from oversight, and lets premarket review raise barriers for newcomers. The dominant firm supported the bill while smaller rivals opposed it [S3][S6].

They face the same registration, disclosure, and premarket review duties as large firms, with testing and manufacturing rules delayed for years to ease the burden; compliance costs still weigh heaviest on them [S3].

The law explicitly excludes tobacco farms, leaf producers, and warehouses from FDA authority — FDA staff cannot even enter a farm without written consent — so growing stays unregulated while manufacturing is controlled [S8].

industries.industry: Flavored cigarette makers (clove and fruit-flavored brands)
industries.note: Candy, fruit, and spice characterizing flavors are banned in cigarettes, wiping out products marketed to young smokers, though menthol — the largest flavored segment — is preserved pending study [S4][S5].

They face advertising restrictions, age-verification rules for remote sales, and possible no-tobacco-sale orders after repeated violations, but the law bars the FDA from banning sales at any category of retail outlet [S3].
